title: Tightly Squeeze Each Muscle Group for Five Seconds, Then Relax It for Thirty Seconds,
subtitle: Progressive Muscle Relaxation (PMR)
description: Tightly squeeze each muscle group for five seconds, then relax it for thirty seconds, moving from your toes up to your head.

lifeOsSource.hack: Tightly squeeze each muscle group for five seconds, then relax it for thirty seconds, moving from your toes up to your head.
lifeOsSource.whatYouDo: Sit or lie somewhere comfortable and work through a few muscle groups one at a time. Gently tense each group for no more than about five seconds, then release it and notice the contrast. Do not strain, and skip or release any area that causes significant discomfort.
lifeOsSource.checkIn: Did I practise without pain or straining? Which areas felt tense, and did I notice any difference after releasing them?
lifeOsSource.reference: Royal Brompton & Harefield hospitals — Progressive muscle relaxation

faq.question: Do I need an exact 5-second tense and 30-second relax timer?
faq.answer: No. NHS sources commonly use a brief tension phase, and Royal Brompton advises holding tension for no more than five seconds before releasing. Brali does not claim that a fixed 30-second release or 35-second cycle is an evidence-based optimum.
faq.answerHtml: No. NHS sources commonly use a brief tension phase, and Royal Brompton advises holding tension for no more than five seconds before releasing. Brali does not claim that a fixed 30-second release or 35-second cycle is an evidence-based optimum.

faq.question: How hard should I tense the muscles?
faq.answer: Only enough to notice the tension without pain or straining. Royal Brompton advises releasing a muscle if tensing it causes significant discomfort. There is no need to target a percentage of maximum force.

faq.question: Is PMR a treatment for depression or anxiety?
faq.answer: Brali presents PMR as a relaxation skill, not as a treatment plan or a guaranteed way to reduce symptoms by a particular amount. If anxiety or low mood is persistent or significantly affects daily life, use appropriate professional support rather than relying on this protocol alone.

intro.html: Progressive muscle relaxation is a simple relaxation exercise built around noticing the difference between muscle tension and release. NHS clinical resources describe moving through major muscle groups, tensing each briefly and then relaxing it. Brali keeps the practice deliberately modest: no percentage promises, no force targets and no claim that one session will produce a predictable mental-health outcome.

sections.title: 1. Get comfortable
sections.html: Sit or lie somewhere you can relax without needing to stay alert to traffic, machinery or another safety-critical task. Let your body be supported and choose a few muscle groups to work through.

sections.title: 2. Tense one muscle group gently
sections.html: Bring one muscle group into noticeable tension without straining. Royal Brompton guidance recommends holding the tension for no more than five seconds. The purpose is awareness, not maximum effort.

sections.title: 3. Release and notice the contrast
sections.html: Let the muscle relax fully and notice the difference between effort and release. There is no required 30-second window. Give yourself enough time to notice the change before moving to the next group.

sections.title: 4. Move through a few groups
sections.html: You can work through areas such as feet and legs, hands and arms, shoulders, jaw and face. You do not need a 12-group or 18-group sequence for the practice to count. Start with a short sequence you can perform comfortably.

sections.title: 5. Use comfort as the boundary
sections.html: If tensing a muscle causes significant discomfort, release it and skip that area. If you have a physical health issue that could make the exercise unsuitable, get appropriate clinical advice before using a general relaxation routine.

sections.title: 6. Review the experience, not a promised effect
sections.html: In Brali, record whether you practised, whether any area was uncomfortable, and what you noticed about tension and release. Do not expect a required percentage improvement in anxiety, tension or sleep. After a few attempts, decide whether PMR is a useful relaxation skill for you.

editorialCuration.reason: Replace an inherited PMR article containing unsupported anxiety/tension percentages, arbitrary force targets, rigid 35-second timing, invented internal observations and treatment-like expectations with a conservative progressive muscle relaxation protocol grounded in current NHS clinical relaxation guidance. The public version presents PMR as a relaxation skill for noticing and releasing muscle tension, not as a treatment for depression or a guaranteed percentage reduction in anxiety.
